---
title: "Contributing"
description: "How to build, test, and land a change — and the conventions the codebase holds itself to."
---

This project is, and always will be, free for everyone. Pull requests, issues, and contributions
are more than encouraged — adding support for another game, fixing a busted call, improving this
wiki, or porting to another platform. The eventual hope is split screen and local co-op working
on all EOS games, regardless of operating system.

## Where things live

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `src/` | The implementation: `core/` (engine), `interfaces/` (EOS interfaces), `flat/` (the C ABI), `net/` (mesh), `common/`, `platform/` (the only OS-specific code) |
| `include/eos/` | Vendored EOS SDK headers (the ABI contract) |
| `tests/` | Unit, integration, trace, and export-surface suites |
| `wiki/` | This website — the [internals section](internals/index.qmd) is the behavioral spec the implementation is built from |
| `tools/`, `scripts/` | The [import census](../users/tracing.qmd#inspect_gamepy-will-this-game-even-load), `test-all.sh` |

Start any interface work by reading its spec page under [Internals](internals/index.qmd) —
the point of this project is that the behavior is *understood first*, then implemented cleanly.

## The golden rules

- **C++11, non-negotiable.** No C++14/17/20 features, ever, and no compiler extensions — the
  build enforces `-std=c++11` strictly. EOS-era games ship with old toolchains, and a drop-in
  library has to build and run beside them. (Note: no `<filesystem>` — that's C++17.)
- **Cross-platform first.** One source tree produces the Windows `.dll` and Linux `.so`. All
  OS-specific code is quarantined in `src/platform/` behind a common header with
  `platform_win32.cpp` / `platform_linux.cpp` implementations; nothing else may include
  `<windows.h>`, `<winsock2.h>`, `<sys/socket.h>`, or friends.
- **Keep dependencies near zero.** Prefer vendoring something small and portable (Monocypher is
  the model: one `.c`/`.h` pair) over pulling a package. The standard library's portable parts —
  containers, `std::thread`, `std::mutex`, `std::chrono`, `std::fstream` — are the toolkit.
- **Simple beats clever.** Readability over optimization; no intrinsics for speed. Prefer early
  returns over nested `if` pyramids. Avoid `std::function`, `std::shared_ptr`, `std::bind`,
  `std::list`: the EOS API is a C ABI of plain function pointers plus `void* ClientData` — use
  that directly, and prefer plain values, `std::unique_ptr`, or clear manual ownership.

## Style, briefly

`snake_case` everywhere — functions, variables, types, files. Four-space indent, no tabs. K&R
braces. `const` whatever can be `const`. No magic numbers — name them with a `constexpr`. Short
Rust-style integer aliases from `src/common/types.h` (`u8`…`u64`, `i8`…`i64`, `f32`, `f64`).
Names anyone can read at a glance (`number`, not `n`).

Comments: fewer is better, "we" not "I", explain the *why* only where the code can't. A one-line
description above a function or a short note before a non-obvious decision is the right amount.

## The test bar

Every change runs the full suite on **both** targets before it lands:

```sh
./scripts/test-all.sh    # native Linux + MinGW-w64 cross under Wine, if installed
```

What green means here: hundreds of unit cases (crypto against published RFC/Noise vectors,
config, identity, every interface), integration tests that load the real built artifact through
the C ABI like a game, a trace-lifecycle test, an export-surface check that nothing beyond
`EOS_*` leaks, and multi-instance mesh e2e — clean under ASan + UBSan.

The project's review culture is **adversarial by default**: an interface lands, then gets
actively attacked against the headers and the spec — forged identities, planted search results,
callback lifetime abuse. Findings become regression tests. Expect (and give) that kind of
review; the [progress manifest](internals/progress.qmd) records what it has caught so far.

## Practical bits

- **CI** is a manual button (Actions → *CI* → Run workflow): it builds native Linux, MinGW cross
  + Wine, and native MSVC, tests all three, and uploads both artifacts. This wiki deploys from
  its own manual workflow the same way.
- **Bug reports**: a [trace](../users/tracing.qmd) plus an
  [import census](../users/troubleshooting.qmd#the-game-wont-launch) makes a report actionable
  in minutes.
- **License**: GPL-3.0. By contributing you agree your work is released under it.
- Keep the [scope](../users/scope.qmd) in mind: contributions aimed at piracy or cheating won't be
  accepted, however technically interesting.
